page.overview:
What is Rhan-Tegoth?

Rhan-Tegoth is a Great Old One in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald for their short story "The Horror in the Museum".

Rhan-Tegoth is an entity shaped somewhat like an enormous insect, with a tremendous, barrel-shaped trunk with six appendages ending in claws-like pincers and a near-spherical head covered with hair-like filaments or feelers, a tentacle-like proboscis and three small, beady eyes. The hair-like feelers function as additional mouths that perforate the skin of the creature's prey and secrete digestive acids. Similar to Chaugnar Faugn, Rhan-Tegoth feeds by sucking out the blood and liquefied innards of its victims, the bodies of which are crushed and disfigured by the great strength of the monster.

Despite being a deity of comparatively little power, it is vital for the return of the Old Ones. It lived in the warm seas of Yuggoth before coming to Earth.

Three million years ago, during the Pliocene epoch, it inhabited an area of Alaska before going into a hibernation-like trance. Rhan-Tegoth was the last god to sleep, and was probably meant to be the first to wake. Its body was found by George Rogers and moved to a museum in London, 1926 (: "The Horror in the Museum"), but was then lost track of until It turned up, firstly in Sheffield, UK in the 1980s (: "The Return of Rhan-Tegoth"), and then in Chorazin, New York in the mid-to-late 1980s. (: "Wilbur Whateley Waiting")​ It was worshipped by the prehuman, cannibal Gnophkehs, but few humans know of it in modern times. (​: "The Scroll of Morloc")
